content:
If arthritis makes it hard to open bottles, pop tablets out of blister foil or handle small pills, start by talking to your pharmacist. They can often give you easy-open tops instead of child-resistant caps, larger labels, or check whether a different form of a medicine would suit you, and they can assess whether a dosette box or pharmacy-filled pack is right for you. These packs suit some people and some medicines but not all, so do not decant tablets into a box yourself without checking. Keep weekly medicines such as methotrexate clearly separate from daily ones, and contact your pharmacist or NHS 111 if you miss doses or take too many. Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself.

This guide is about the physical side of taking tablets when your hands are painful, stiff or weak. If the main problem is remembering doses, or you take a lot of different medicines, see getting a pharmacist medication review and painkillers in later life.

Why medicines get harder with arthritis in the hands

  • Child-resistant caps need a push-and-twist that hurts with thumb and finger arthritis.
  • Blister packs need a strong pinch and push through the foil.
  • Small tablets are hard to pick up, and easy to drop and lose.
  • Eye drops, inhalers, creams and injections each need a different kind of grip.

If any of this means you skip doses, take them late or ask a neighbour to open everything, tell your pharmacist or GP. There is usually a simpler way.

Start with your pharmacist

Your community pharmacist is the best first stop. You do not need an appointment for a quick chat, and many pharmacies have a private room. Ask about:

  • Easy-open tops instead of child-resistant caps, if there are no young children in your home or visiting.
  • Large-print labels or an extra information sheet.
  • A different form of the medicine, such as a liquid, a larger tablet or a once-daily version. Only your prescriber can change this, but the pharmacist can suggest it to them.
  • Whether your medicines can go in a dosette box or a pharmacy-filled pack, and whether there is a charge. Under the Equality Act 2010, services have to make reasonable adjustments for disabled people, so explain clearly how your hands affect you.
  • Help with a new medicine. In England, the NHS New Medicine Service gives you extra support from a pharmacist when you start some new medicines.

Dosette boxes and pharmacy-filled packs

A dosette box (also called a pill organiser) has compartments for each day and time. Some pharmacies fill sealed weekly packs for you. They can make tablets easier to manage, but they are not right for everyone.

What can work well

  • Seeing at a glance whether you have taken today's tablets.
  • Large compartments with sliding or flip lids that are easy to open with a knuckle.
  • A box where each day clicks out, so you can take one day with you.

What to check first

  • Not every medicine can go in a box. Some tablets go off when taken out of their original packaging, and medicines you take only when needed, liquids, inhalers and some soluble tablets usually stay separate. Ask the pharmacist before putting anything in.
  • Sealed packs can be just as hard to open as blister foil. Try one in the pharmacy before you commit.
  • Changes need care. If your doctor stops or changes a medicine, the box or pack needs to change too. Tell your pharmacist about every change, including after a hospital stay.
  • Weekly medicines such as methotrexate must be kept clearly separate. The NHS says methotrexate for arthritis is taken once a week, and taking it every day by mistake can be very dangerous. Keep it in its own box and mark your weekly day on it.

NICE guidance on medicines optimisation (NG5) and on managing medicines in social care (NG67) says compliance aids such as these should only be used after the person's needs have been looked at, and that other options, like simpler regimens or easy-open packaging, should be considered too.

Small aids that help

  • Blister pack openers (tablet poppers) push tablets out of the foil with very little pressure.
  • Bottle and cap openers with a rubber grip, or a non-slip mat under the bottle.
  • A shallow dish or saucer to tip tablets into, so they do not roll away.
  • Pill cutters and crushers only if your pharmacist says that tablet can be split or crushed. Many cannot.
  • Eye drop and inhaler aids. Ask your pharmacist or nurse; there are dispensers that need less squeezing.

Many of these cost little. See gadgets and aids for arthritis for more ideas, and joint protection for ways to spare painful hands.

Reminders and help from others

  • A phone alarm, a smart speaker or a written chart next to the box can help if you also find it hard to remember doses.
  • Some councils and telecare services offer automatic pill dispensers that open at set times. Ask about these at a care needs assessment. The NHS says having a needs assessment is free, and equipment and small adaptations will be provided for free if you are assessed as needing them.
  • If family or care workers help, agree who fills the box and who orders repeat prescriptions, so nothing is missed or doubled up. Paid carers follow a care plan for medicines support.

Treating the hands themselves

Hand exercises, splints and the right pain relief can make gripping easier. See hand osteoarthritis: easier dressing and grip and hand exercises for arthritis. An occupational therapist can also look at how you manage medicines and suggest equipment. See occupational therapy for arthritis.

If remembering tablets is getting harder

Memory changes, tiredness or several new medicines can make it easy to miss or double a dose. A pill organiser helps many people, but it is only one option.

  • Ask your pharmacist whether your medicines can be simplified or taken at fewer times of day.
  • Phone alarms, a tick chart or a family member checking in can help alongside a dosette box.
  • If you or your family notice new or worsening memory problems, mention this to your GP.

When to get help

  • Contact your pharmacist or NHS 111 if you have missed several doses, are not sure whether you have taken a dose, or think you have taken too many. Have the packets with you.
  • Call 999 if someone has taken a lot more than prescribed and is very drowsy, confused or having trouble breathing.
  • Tell your GP if your hands are getting worse quickly, or if new swelling, numbness or tingling is making tablets harder to handle.

Common questions

Can I fill my own dosette box?

Many people do, but check with your pharmacist first which of your medicines are safe to take out of their packaging, and keep the original boxes so you have the details.

Will the pharmacy charge for a filled pack?

It depends on the pharmacy and on your needs. Ask, and explain how your arthritis affects your hands.

Is it safe to keep tablets out of their packets for a week?

For many tablets yes, but not all. Your pharmacist can tell you which ones need to stay in their original packaging.
